summary: The Seto Inland Sea between Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu: island-studded straits, old port towns, granite hills with sea views and the tidal whirlpools of Naruto. One of Japan's first three national parks, and with its waters its largest, it takes in Miyajima's shrine, the art islands, the Shimanami Kaidō cycle route and fragments of coast and sea across eleven prefectures.
story: Between Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu lies a shallow sea scattered with around three thousand islands, and the park is spread across it in pieces. The tide, forced through the narrow straits between the islands, runs hard: at Naruto, between Awaji Island and Shikoku, it spins into whirlpools, and at Funaori Seto in the central islands it boils at the change of tide. Much of the rock is granite, weathered on hills such as Washūzan and Rokkō into rounded crags, and worn down into pale beaches backed by pines.

Sheltered by the mountains of Chūgoku and Shikoku, the region has a mild, fairly dry climate, often compared with the Mediterranean, and Shōdoshima was where Japan first grew olives. The sea is rich. Finless porpoises feed in the channels, Japanese horseshoe crabs live on the mudflats of Okayama, salt-marsh plants grow along its shores, and Miyajima's small wetlands shelter the Miyajima dragonfly.

For centuries this sea was one of Japan's great highways, and its ports grew on the traffic. Tomonoura, where ships waited for wind and tide, still has its old harbour, temples and merchant houses, and the Murakami sea lords of the central islands are remembered in a museum on Ōshima. Itsukushima Shrine on Miyajima, built over the tide flats with its great torii standing in the sea, became a World Heritage Site in 1996. Since the 1980s Naoshima, Teshima and Inujima have become places of contemporary art.

On 16 March 1934 Setonaikai became, with Unzen and Kirishima, one of Japan's first three national parks. It began small, with only the classic viewpoints of the Bisan Seto — Kankakei on Shōdoshima, Yashima, Washūzan and Tomonoura — and grew in 1950 and 1956 to cover scattered coast and islands from Kobe to Kitakyushu and Ōita. Much of the wider sea industrialised fast after the war, and the park is in part a record of what was saved.
howItWorks: Setonaikai is the clearest example of a Japanese regional park. It is not a single tract of wild land but dozens of separate pieces — hills above cities, islands, headlands, beaches and historic harbours — strung across the sea, and about 72 per cent of the land is privately owned. People live and work throughout it: fishing ports, island villages, temples, shrines, orchards and resort towns all lie inside the boundary, and ferries, bridges and shipping lanes cross it.

Protection comes from zoning. Only about 1.5 per cent of the land is special protection zone. Around two-thirds is special zone, in three classes, where buildings, quarrying, felling and changes to the shoreline need permission and must fit the landscape; the remaining third is ordinary zone, where large works need only notice. At sea, four small marine park zones were designated off the islands of Yamaguchi Prefecture in 2013.

Other designations overlap the park. Itsukushima Shrine is a World Heritage Site, and Miyajima's wetlands are a Ramsar site. On Miyajima, Hatsukaichi City levies a visitor tax collected with the ferry fare. Many viewpoints are also national scenic places, and the art sites of Naoshima and its neighbours grew from a private corporate project.

sights.name: Itsukushima and Mount Misen (厳島・弥山)
sights.note: Miyajima's shrine and its torii standing in the tide, with trails and a ropeway up Mount Misen behind. A World Heritage Site; stay overnight to see it quiet.

sights.name: Naruto Strait (鳴門海峡)
sights.note: Tidal whirlpools between Awaji Island and Shikoku, formed as the tide races through the narrow strait. Sightseeing boats run out to them.

sights.name: Washūzan (鷲羽山)
sights.note: A granite hill at the tip of the Kojima Peninsula, one of the park's original viewpoints, looking over the islands of the Bisan Seto and the Seto Ōhashi bridges.

sights.name: Kankakei (寒霞渓)
sights.note: A rocky gorge in the mountains of Shōdoshima; one of the original 1934 sites.

sights.name: Yashima (屋島)
sights.note: A flat-topped hill above Takamatsu with views over the islands; one of the original 1934 sites.

sights.name: Tomonoura and Sensuijima (鞆の浦・仙酔島)
sights.note: A historic port where ships once waited for the tide, and the wild island just offshore with coloured volcanic rocks and a beach.

sights.name: Mount Rokkō (六甲山)
sights.note: The granite range behind Kobe; its 931-metre summit looks over the city, Osaka Bay and the sea.

sights.name: Shimanami Kaidō (しまなみ海道)
sights.note: A 70-kilometre cycle route over six islands between Onomichi and Imabari. From Kirōsan on Ōshima, look down on the Kurushima Strait, where tides reach about 10 knots.

sights.name: Goshikidai Visitor Center
sights.note: On the Goshikidai uplands between Takamatsu and Sakaide, looking over the Bisan Seto.

sights.name: Ōkunoshima Visitor Center
sights.note: On Ōkunoshima, a small island off Takehara in Hiroshima Prefecture.

entrances: Miyajimaguchi on the JR Sanyō Line, with ferries to Miyajima
Okayama and Uno, with ferries to Naoshima and Shōdoshima
Onomichi and Imabari, at either end of the Shimanami Kaidō
Takamatsu, for Yashima, Goshikidai and the islands of Kagawa
Naruto and Awaji Island, for the whirlpools
planYourVisit.reservations: No park permit or entry booking is needed. Ferries to the art islands and accommodation on Miyajima and Naoshima fill up at weekends, in holiday periods and during the Setouchi Triennale; check timetables and book ahead.
camping: Campsites on several islands and beaches, among them Keino-matsubara on Awaji Island
lodging: Inns on Miyajima, Shōdoshima, Naoshima and along the Shimanami Kaidō
Hotels in Hiroshima, Okayama, Takamatsu, Onomichi, Imabari and Kobe

weather: The Inland Sea has one of the mildest, driest climates in Japan, sheltered by the mountains of Chūgoku to the north and Shikoku to the south. Winters are cool and mostly sunny, with little snow at sea level. Spring is the classic season, with cherry blossom in late March and early April. The rainy season runs from June into July, and summer is hot and humid, with typhoons possible from August to October. Autumn is clear and settled, with colour in the hills from November.
directions: The Tokaido–Sanyō Shinkansen runs along the Honshu shore from Shin-Osaka to Kokura, stopping at Shin-Kobe, Okayama, Fukuyama, Shin-Onomichi and Hiroshima, which are the gateways to most of the park. For Miyajima, take the JR Sanyō Line from Hiroshima to Miyajimaguchi (about 30 minutes) and a JR or Matsudai ferry across (about 10 minutes). For Naoshima, take the JR Uno Line from Okayama to Uno and a ferry from Uno Port; Shōdoshima has ferries from Shin-Okayama, Hinase and Uno. The Shimanami Kaidō starts at Onomichi, where bicycles can be hired and dropped at points along the way. Shikoku is reached by rail over the Seto Ōhashi from Okayama to Takamatsu, and Awaji Island by road over the Akashi Kaikyō Bridge. Airports at Hiroshima, Okayama, Takamatsu, Matsuyama, Yamaguchi-Ube, Kitakyushu and Ōita serve the far ends.

fees.title: Miyajima Visitor Tax
fees.detail: Levied by Hatsukaichi City on each visit to Miyajima since 1 October 2023, collected with the ferry fare. An annual payment of ¥500 is an alternative. Residents, preschool children and some others are exempt.

chronology.text: On 16 March Setonaikai becomes one of Japan's first three national parks, together with Unzen and Kirishima, covering the Bisan Seto around Shōdoshima, Yashima, Washūzan and Tomonoura.
The park is greatly enlarged east and west along the Inland Sea.
A further extension adds more of the coast and islands, including Takasakiyama in Ōita.
Itsukushima Shrine is inscribed as a World Heritage Site.
The first Setouchi Triennale art festival is held on the islands.
The park's first marine park zones are designated, off the islands of Yamaguchi Prefecture.
Hatsukaichi City begins collecting a visitor tax on Miyajima.

safety: Tidal currents in the straits are fast and change direction with the tide. Do not swim near straits or harbour mouths, and kayak only with local knowledge of the tides.
On the Shimanami Kaidō, bridges are long and exposed to wind; walk your bicycle in strong gusts and watch for traffic at the island junctions.
Typhoons from August to October can cancel ferries for a day or more. Allow slack in island itineraries.
Summer heat is severe on shadeless islands; carry water when cycling or walking.
regulations: Do not feed the deer on Miyajima.
Collecting plants, animals and rocks is restricted in the special zones; in the marine park zones, collecting designated marine life needs permission.
Shellfish and seaweed on the shore belong to local fishing cooperatives; gathering them without a right is poaching.
On Miyajima, the visitor tax is payable on each visit, normally with the ferry fare.
